newsitem.title: INDIA: I-Sec sees India 1996/97 GDP growth around 6.0 pct.
newsitem.headline: I-Sec sees India 1996/97 GDP growth around 6.0 pct.

text.p: ICICI Securities and Finance Company (I-Sec) said on Wednesday that it expected India's 1996/97 (April-March) GDP growth to be around 6.0 percent against the government's target of 7.0 percent.
"It would not be unreasonable to believe that we would end 1996/97 financial year with a real growth rate close to 6.0 percent than 7.0 percent as budgeted," it said in a report.
It said a lower growth rate this year was inevitable.

"From the current point in time, it seems very unlikely that interest rates would decline sharply in the second half of 1996 to induce investments, unless a significant amount of foreign savings are directed towards the Indian debt markets," it said.
I-Sec said Indian investors are currently having a boom time with yields in excess of 18 percent for the top rated Indian companies.

"However, a note of caution needs to be sounded since the high real cost of mobilising domestic savings will certainly put a severe strain on corporate bottom lines and a higher frequency of downgrading of credit ratings should not come as a surprise," I-Sec, the Indian affiliate of J.P. Morgan, said.
The State Bank of India, followed by several other banks, raised their prime lending rates in recent weeks to 15.5 percent from 16 percent a year.
"While it is evident that the rate cut has been induced by sluggish credit growth, it remains to be seen if a 50 basis point cut would be sufficient to fuel credit a pick up," it said.
It said the central bank was concerned over recessionary developments and "what needs to be done is to give a jolt to interest rate expectations".
This could be in the form of a fresh cut in the cash reserve ratio of banks, which would enable banks to further reduce their lending rates, I-Sec said.

"Deposit rates of 15 percent on longer maturities offered by some banks are too high and need to decline if their spreads are to be protected without sacrificing the credit quality of assets," I-Sec debt research manager Aashish Pitale said.
